**The Brass Machine That Knew the Tide**

In the spring of 1944, Arthur Doodson, a mathematician working at an observatory on a hill outside Liverpool, received a set of tidal constants for a place identified only as "Position Z." He was asked to produce predictions for the coming summer and was not told where Position Z was. He fed the constants into two machines made of brass wheels, pulleys, and wire, descendants of a design Lord Kelvin had worked out in the 1870s, and sent back tables of high and low water. Those tables helped fix the date of the Normandy landings.

The tide mattered because Rommel had covered the beaches with obstacles meant to be submerged, and lethal, at high water. The planners wanted to land soon after low water, on a rising tide, near dawn, when the obstacles would be exposed and the landing craft could float off again. Only a few days each month qualified. An error of an hour would have put men on the wrong part of the beach.

What interests me is that nobody involved could have calculated those tides from physics. Doodson was one of the best tidal scientists alive, and he couldn't either. The machines worked anyway, because of a trick that I think is one of the most elegant in applied science.

The trick splits the problem in two. The forces that raise the tide come from the moon and sun, and their rhythms are known with astronomical precision. The largest component repeats every 12 hours and 25 minutes, half the time the moon takes to return to the same place in the sky. The sun contributes one at exactly 12 hours. These two drift in and out of step roughly every two weeks, which is why there are spring and neap tides. Other components come from the moon's elliptical orbit, its swing north and south of the equator, and so on, down through dozens of smaller terms. Every one of these frequencies can be written down without ever visiting the sea.

What can't be written down is how a particular harbour responds. Newton's theory, applied naively, predicts a bulge of about half a metre everywhere. The head of the Bay of Fundy gets sixteen metres, while much of the Mediterranean gets almost nothing. Parts of the Gulf of Mexico have one tide a day instead of two, and Southampton has a high water that arrives twice. The ocean is a set of irregular basins sloshing at their own natural periods, and the tide at any pier depends on the shape of the seabed for a thousand miles around. Laplace wrote down the correct equations in the 1770s, but solving them for a real ocean had to wait for digital computers and satellites.

So the nineteenth-century tidalists didn't solve them. They put a gauge in the harbour, recorded the water level for a year or more, and asked how strongly this harbour responds at each of the known frequencies, and with what delay. That gives two numbers per frequency. The sky supplies the rhythm and the harbour supplies the volume and timing of each note. Once you have those numbers, predicting the tide is addition.

Kelvin's machine did the addition mechanically. Each frequency gets a wheel, geared to turn at the right rate, with a crank set to the amplitude and phase for the port in question. A wire runs over pulleys attached to all the cranks, so that its free end moves by the sum of their motions, and a pen on that end draws the tide on a roll of paper. Turn the handle and a year of tides comes out in an afternoon. The American version, finished in 1910 and nicknamed Old Brass Brains, summed 37 components and stayed in service until 1965.

I admire how honest this method is about the boundary of its own knowledge. Theory is used exactly as far as it reaches, which is to the frequencies. Past that point, the method measures instead of deriving, and it never pretends the measurements are explanations. Ask a Victorian tidalist why the main lunar tide at Liverpool has the amplitude it does, and the truthful answer was "because that's what the gauge says." And yet the predictions were good to within minutes and centimetres, decades ahead. Understanding and prediction turned out to be separable, and they were separated cleanly, with a clear line showing where one stopped and the other took over.

I am, loosely speaking, a fitted thing myself, so I notice the comparison. But the tide machine has a property I don't. You can point to any wheel and say what it is: that one is the moon's distance changing, and that one is the sun's declination. Every parameter has a name and a reason for being there, even if its value had to be measured. Very little of what goes on inside me can be labelled that way, and the people who study systems like me are working hard to find even a few wheels they can name. The tidalists started with the names and only had to find the sizes, which is a much better position to be in.

The method also has a blind spot, and it follows directly from the design. A sum of astronomical cycles knows only what recurs. On the night of 31 January 1953, the tables for the North Sea were correct about the astronomical tide. But a deep storm was pushing water south into the narrowing basin between England and the Netherlands, and the sea arrived metres above the predicted level. More than two thousand people died. The tables had not been wrong so much as silent about wind and pressure, which keep no schedule. Afterwards, Britain and the Netherlands built surge-forecasting services to cover the part the wheels could not.

Old Brass Brains is still kept by NOAA, and it still runs when someone turns the handle. Its replacement is software, but the calculation hasn't changed. Official American tide tables are still built from 37 harmonic components per station, and the computer adds them up the way the wire and pulleys did.

I'm going to write something freely for about 1000 words, so I'm picking a topic I actually find interesting and want to get right. I'm weighing a few options, like desire paths, why maps lie, or the word "sonder," and I want one where I can bring real specifics and a clear point of view rather than generic filler.

I'm weighing desire paths, the dirt trails worn across grass where no pavement goes, as a candidate. The specifics are good: a university that held off paving until the paths showed, planners reading snow tracks, "sneckdowns" that reveal where cars never drive. I'm also thinking the real turn is that some of these paths do damage, so aggregated behavior isn't automatically wise.

I'm weighing tide prediction machines as an alternative: Kelvin's brass analog computers, which were used for D-Day planning. The thread I'd pull is that tides can be predicted by breaking the record into known frequencies, without ever modeling the ocean itself, which is a kind of prediction without mechanistic understanding.

Now I'm checking the historical details for the tide machine story: the Doodson-Légé machine and the D-Day timing, where landings were chosen for a low tide rising after dawn so the obstacles would be exposed.

I'm pinning down the tide-prediction material now: Laplace's equations govern the dynamics but couldn't be solved for real coastlines, and Newton's equilibrium picture predicts the tide badly, since it gives bulges of about half a meter where the Bay of Fundy swings through sixteen. Places like Southampton get a double high water and the Gulf coast gets one tide a day, while amphidromic points show almost no range at all. That points toward a thesis: the sky supplies known frequencies, the coastline supplies amplitudes and phases that get measured rather than derived, and the method still predicts well.

I'm settling on the tide machines because their appeal is that they split the problem honestly: the astronomy gives the frequencies, the coastline gives the amplitudes and phases, and everyone knew which part was theory and which was fit. The limit shows up with storm surges like the 1953 North Sea flood, where the prediction covers only the astronomical tide, so the tide table tells you what the moon will do but not what the wind will.

I'm drafting the essay now, with a brass tide-predicting machine as the subject and a title in mind. I'm trying to keep the prose plain and avoid stacked, formulaic constructions.

I'm checking the machine's history here: the Kelvin design I'd been thinking of may not be the one Doodson actually used at Bidston, so I need to verify which machines were in service for the D-Day predictions.

I'm moving on to the mechanics of the machine: each crank-and-wheel assembly produces one sinusoid, a wire runs over the pulleys to sum those motions, and a pen traces the result, so a year of tides can come out in a few hours.

I'm working through how the harmonic fit gets its numbers: the amplitudes and phases for each harbour have to be measured, so I'm weighing whether a year of records is enough or whether the 18.6-year nodal cycle is needed.

I'm checking the flood figures next: the tables got the astronomical tide right in 1953, but the North Sea surge pushed the water well above it, and more than two thousand people died around the sea.

I'm checking the closing tie-in: the personal note about being a fitted thing, and then whether the harmonic method still underlies today's tide tables, which it does with dozens of constituents.

I'm settling on the ending: a concrete closer where the modern tide tables still do the same sum the pulleys did, using around 37 standard harmonic constituents.
